title: Alopecia areata
description: Loss of hair from areas on the body
wiki_lead:
Alopecia areata (AA), also known as spot baldness, is a condition in which hair is lost from some or all areas of the body. It often results in a few bald spots on the scalp, each about the size of a coin. Psychological stress and illness are possible factors in bringing on alopecia areata in individuals at risk, but in most cases there is no obvious trigger. People are generally otherwise healthy. In a few cases, all the hair on the scalp is lost (alopecia totalis), or all body hair is lost (alopecia universalis). Hair loss can be permanent or temporary.
Alopecia areata is believed to be an autoimmune disease resulting from a breach in the immune privilege of the hair follicles. Risk factors include a family history of the condition. Among identical twins, if one is affected, the other has about a 50% chance of also being affected. The underlying mechanism involves failure by the body to recognize its own cells, with subsequent immune-mediated destruction of the hair follicle.
No cure for the condition is known. Some treatments, particularly triamcinolone injections and 5% minoxidil topical creams, are effective in speeding hair regrowth. Sunscreen, head coverings to protect from cold and sun, and glasses, if the eyelashes are missing, are also recommended. In more than 50% of cases of sudden-onset localized "patchy" disease, hair regrows within a year. In patients with only one or two patches, this one-year recovery will occur in up to 80%. However, many people will have more than one episode over the course of a lifetime. In many patients, hair loss and regrowth occurs simultaneously over the course of several years. Among those in whom all body hair is lost, fewer than 10% recover without treatment.
About 0.15% of people are affected at any one time, and 2% of people are affected at some point in time. Onset is usually in childhood. Females are affected at higher rates than males.

Signs and symptoms

Typical first symptoms of alopecia areata are small bald patches. The underlying skin is unscarred and looks superficially normal. Although these patches can take many shapes, they are usually round or oval. Alopecia areata most often affects the scalp and beard, but may occur on any part of the body with hair. Different areas of the skin may exhibit hair loss and regrowth at the same time. The disease may also go into remission for a time, or may be permanent. It is common in children.
The area of hair loss may tingle or be mildly painful. The hair tends to fall out over a short period of time, with the loss commonly occurring more on one side of the scalp than the other.
Exclamation point hairs, narrower along the length of the strand closer to the base, producing a characteristic "exclamation point" appearance, are often present. These hairs are very short (3–4 mm; 0.1–0.2 in), and can be seen surrounding the bald patches.

grok_lead: Alopecia areata is a common autoimmune disorder characterized by sudden, nonscarring hair loss in round, smooth patches, most often on the scalp but potentially affecting any hair-bearing area of the body, resulting from the immune system's mistaken attack on hair follicles. The condition arises from a disruption in the immune privilege of hair follicles, where T cells infiltrate and trigger an inflammatory response via cytokines such as interferon-gamma and interleukin-15, leading to premature transition from the growth (anagen) phase to the resting (telogen) phase of the hair cycle. Genetic predisposition plays a significant role, with multiple genes associated with immune regulation implicated, alongside environmental triggers like stress or infections that may precipitate onset in susceptible individuals. It affects approximately 2% of the population over a lifetime, with a prevalence of about 1 in 1,000, occurring across all age groups but most commonly starting before age 40, and showing higher rates in Asian, Black, and Hispanic populations. Symptoms typically include one or more well-demarcated bald patches, often with short, tapered " exclamation mark " hairs at the periphery, and may extend to the beard (alopecia barbae), eyebrows, or body hair; in about 10-15% of cases, nail changes such as pitting or ridging occur. The disease manifests in varying severity: patchy alopecia areata (most common, limited to discrete areas), alopecia totalis (complete scalp hair loss), alopecia universalis (total body hair loss, rare), and alopecia ophiasis (band-like loss along the scalp margins, associated with poorer prognosis). Diagnosis is primarily clinical, supported by dermoscopy revealing yellow dots or cadaverized hairs, and biopsy if needed to rule out differentials such as tinea capitis, trichotillomania, or vitamin/nutritional deficiencies. Treatment aims to suppress the autoimmune response and promote regrowth, as there is no cure; options include intralesional corticosteroid injections (first-line for patchy disease, effective in up to 80% for mild cases), topical corticosteroids or minoxidil, contact immunotherapy (e.g., diphencyprone), and systemic Janus kinase (JAK) inhibitors like baricitinib (FDA-approved 2022), ritlecitinib (FDA-approved 2023), or deuruxolitinib (FDA-approved 2024), which target the JAK-STAT pathway and have shown significant efficacy in severe cases. In cases where alopecia areata co-occurs with androgenetic alopecia, treatments for both conditions can be pursued simultaneously due to their distinct etiologies and mechanisms. Spontaneous regrowth occurs in about 50% of patients within one year, though relapse is common (up to 80% within five years), with worse outcomes for early childhood onset, extensive involvement, or ophiasis pattern. The condition is not contagious and, while primarily cosmetic, can cause significant emotional distress, underscoring the importance of multidisciplinary care involving dermatologists and support resources.
